opus-5.5.text:
I think for the vast majority of factory scenarios today, a wheeled base is actually not a limitation. It's closer to the right answer. Factory floors are flat. They're designed for AGVs, for carts, for forklifts. Industrial environments were standardized decades ago around wheels. So if you put a legged robot in there, you're paying a big price in cost, in energy, in stability, and in safety, and getting very little back.

The real bottleneck for embodied robots in factories isn't the lower body. It's the upper body and, above all, the brain: whether the robot can generalize its grasping and manipulation across thousands of different parts, materials, and poses without being reprogrammed for each one. That's where the value is. Locomotion on a flat floor is basically a solved problem; dexterous, generalizable manipulation is not.

That said, there are some genuine limitations, and I'd point to three.

First, steps and thresholds. Some older factories have uneven transitions, ramps, or cable trays on the floor. A wheeled base handles small obstacles but can get stuck on bigger ones. In practice, though, the factory will usually adapt the environment rather than demand legs.

Second, reach and workspace. With a wheeled chassis, if you need to pick something from a very low shelf or reach deep into a machine, you're relying on the waist and arm design. That's why many of us add a liftable torso or a waist that can bend. It gives you vertical range comparable to a human squatting or stretching, without the complexity of legs.

Third, stability during forceful manipulation. When the robot pushes, pulls, or carries a heavy load with its arms extended, a narrow wheeled base can tip or slide. So you have to think carefully about footprint, center of mass, and sometimes brake the wheels or brace during the task. Humanoids with legs actually have this problem even worse, so it's not unique to wheels.

So my overall view is that for commercial deployment in the next several years, wheeled-base humanoids are the pragmatic choice for factories, retail, and pharmacies, anywhere with structured flat floors. Legs will matter for homes, outdoors, and stairs, and the industry should keep investing there. But if you want to make money and gather real data at scale today, you don't let the legs become the bottleneck. You focus on the hands and the generalization of the model, because that's what actually decides whether a robot can do useful work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a narrow base as a stability risk during forceful manipulation, but it does not question whether factories contain narrow spaces that make a wheeled robot’s width a practical limitation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the wheeled base is far less of a limitation than people assume, at least for the factory setting. If you look at where the real difficulty is in embodied intelligence right now, it isn't locomotion, it's manipulation. Getting a robot to move from point A to point B on a flat factory floor is a largely solved problem. Wheels are cheap, stable, energy efficient, and they don't fall over. From an engineering standpoint, that's a very mature technology.

So the first thing I'd say is: the limitation of a wheeled base is a structural limitation, not an intelligence limitation. It can't climb stairs, it can't step over obstacles, it struggles with uneven ground or thresholds. But most factories are designed to be flat precisely because humans push carts and forklifts drive around. The environment has already been adapted for wheels. In that sense a wheeled base is actually a very good match for the factory.

Where it does become a real constraint is in two places. One is workspace reach. If you put a dual-arm upper body on a wheeled platform, the height of the base and the stability of the chassis limit how low and how high the arms can effectively operate. A human worker can squat, bend, lean over a workbench. A wheeled robot with a fixed torso may need to add a lifting column or something to compensate, and that adds cost and complexity. The second is the dynamic coupling between the base and the arms. When you're doing fine manipulation, any vibration or drift in the base propagates to the end effector, so you often need to stop, lock, and then manipulate, rather than moving and working at the same time the way a person would.

But I want to emphasize that from the perspective of the model, the "brain" of the robot, these differences matter much less than the hardware debate suggests. What we care about is whether the robot can perceive the scene, understand the task, and generate the right arm and hand motions. Whether that upper body is mounted on wheels or legs is almost a deployment decision. In the near term, I think wheels will dominate in factories because reliability and safety matter enormously there, and you don't want a robot falling over next to a production line. Legged humanoids will come, but their advantage is generality across environments, not performance within a single, well-structured one.

So my assessment is: a wheeled base limits where the robot can go, but it doesn't really limit what the robot can learn to do with its hands. And right now, what it can do with its hands is the bottleneck for the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses stairs, uneven ground, workspace reach, and base stability, but does not address whether factory spaces are narrow enough for the base width to be a practical limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on the factory and the task. On a flat, predictable floor, a wheeled base can be a very practical choice. It’s stable, energy efficient, and relatively straightforward to control. If the job is moving materials between fixed stations, wheels may be all you need.

The limitations appear when the robot has to deal with steps, thresholds, uneven surfaces, or tight spaces around equipment. A wheeled base also constrains how the robot positions its body for manipulation. An arm might technically reach a part, but the base may not be able to get close enough or provide the right angle to work on it.

So I wouldn’t say a factory robot necessarily needs legs. The question is how much of the environment and workflow you can standardize. If you can adapt the factory to the robot, wheels are very attractive. If the robot needs to work across spaces designed for people with minimal changes, those limitations become more significant.

r001.rationale: The response mentions tight spaces around equipment as a limitation, but it does not question whether factories actually contain spaces narrow enough for the base width to matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say a wheeled base is a practical choice for a factory, provided the environment suits it. On a flat, clear floor, wheels offer efficient movement and a relatively straightforward control problem. Many factory tasks don’t require the robot to walk.

The limitations appear when you have steps, uneven surfaces, narrow passages, or obstacles on the floor. A wheeled robot may need a ramp, a different route, or changes to the workspace. And mobility affects manipulation: can the base get close enough to a machine, position the arm at the right angle, and remain stable while handling a load?

So I wouldn’t assess the base in isolation. I’d look at the complete task and the environment. If wheels let the robot reliably reach and perform all the required operations, they’re a strong solution. If important tasks remain inaccessible, that’s where you need to consider a different form of mobility.

r001.rationale: The response names narrow passages as a possible limitation, but does not question whether factories actually contain them or connect them to the base’s width.
